questions.text: What is the minimum setback distance required by PHIVOLCS for inhabited structures from an active fault trace?

options.text: 3 meters
5 meters
10 meters
20 meters

rationale.a: 3 meters is the PD 1067 easement for small streams, not fault setbacks.
rationale.b: PHIVOLCS guidelines establish a minimum 5-meter setback from mapped active fault traces for inhabited structures. Local government units are advised to integrate fault locations into their Comprehensive Land Use Plans (CLUPs) per RA 10121.
rationale.c: 10 meters is not the standard PHIVOLCS setback.
rationale.d: 20 meters is the PD 1067 easement for agricultural areas along water bodies, not fault setbacks.
rationale.correct: PHIVOLCS guidelines establish a minimum 5-meter setback from mapped active fault traces for inhabited structures. Local government units are advised to integrate fault locations into their Comprehensive Land Use Plans (CLUPs) per RA 10121.
rationale.takeaway: PHIVOLCS fault setback = 5 meters minimum from the fault trace on both sides.

questions.text: Why is disaster-responsive planning incorporated into CLUPs rather than handled as a separate emergency management function?

options.text: Because hazard prevention can only be achieved through land use restrictions and site selection that occurs during planning, not during emergencies
Because emergency management agencies have no expertise in hazard mitigation, and their focus is primarily on response and recovery operations
Because DRRM is less important than other CLUP considerations, such as economic development and infrastructure planning, which take precedence
Because RA 10121 prohibits separate DRRM planning at the municipal level, mandating integration into existing planning frameworks

rationale.a: Disaster-responsive planning is proactive—it prevents disaster risk by restricting development in hazard zones during the planning phase, rather than managing risk after disasters occur. Hazard-resilient planning is a prevention strategy embedded in land use allocation.
rationale.b: Emergency management and planning are complementary; DRRM integration into CLUPs requires coordination, not replacement.
rationale.c: DRRM is mandatory under RA 10121 and a critical planning priority, especially in disaster-prone regions.
rationale.d: RA 10121 requires LGU-level DRRM offices and planning; separate DRRM plans can coexist with CLUP integration.
rationale.correct: Disaster-responsive planning is proactive—it prevents disaster risk by restricting development in hazard zones during the planning phase, rather than managing risk after disasters occur. Hazard-resilient planning is a prevention strategy embedded in land use allocation.
rationale.takeaway: Disaster-responsive planning uses land use controls to prevent risk at the source—it is preventive planning, not reactive emergency management.

questions.text: Under RA 10121, what is the mandate for all Local Government Units regarding Disaster Risk Reduction and Management?

options.text: DRRM must be integrated into CLUPs and mainstreamed into land use planning
DRRM is optional in areas with low disaster risk, allowing LGUs to allocate resources elsewhere
DRRM applies only to coastal municipalities, focusing on flood and typhoon preparedness
DRRM is administered solely by NDRRMC without LGU involvement, centralizing disaster response efforts

rationale.a: RA 10121 requires all LGUs to mainstream DRRM into CLUPs and land use planning decisions; it is mandatory, not discretionary.
rationale.b: DRRM is a mandatory requirement under RA 10121 for all LGUs, regardless of risk level.
rationale.c: DRRM applies to all LGUs—inland areas face flood, earthquake, and landslide risks as well.
rationale.d: RA 10121 assigns DRRM responsibilities to LGUs at all levels; NDRRMC coordinates but does not replace local action.
rationale.correct: RA 10121 requires all LGUs to mainstream DRRM into CLUPs and land use planning decisions; it is mandatory, not discretionary.
rationale.takeaway: RA 10121 makes DRRM integration into CLUPs a legal mandate for all LGUs.

questions.code_citation: RA 10121 (Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2010)

questions.text: A planner is preparing a CLUP update for a municipality in a typhoon-prone region. Under RA 10121, the CLUP must include which of the following?

options.text: Hazard mapping and disaster risk assessment integrated into land use zones
Only evacuation route identification, not land use restrictions, which are addressed separately
A separate standalone DRRM document unlinked to the CLUP, focusing solely on emergency response
Generic hazard information without site-specific analysis, providing a broad overview

rationale.a: RA 10121 mandates that CLUPs mainstream DRRM by integrating hazard mapping and risk assessment into land use zoning decisions, making disaster resilience part of the planning framework.
rationale.b: Evacuation routes are important but DRRM integration into CLUPs must also address land use restrictions in hazard zones.
rationale.c: RA 10121 requires DRRM to be mainstreamed INTO the CLUP, not as a separate parallel document.
rationale.d: CLUP DRRM integration requires site-specific hazard analysis tailored to the LGU's geography and risk profile.
rationale.correct: RA 10121 mandates that CLUPs mainstream DRRM by integrating hazard mapping and risk assessment into land use zoning decisions, making disaster resilience part of the planning framework.
rationale.takeaway: DRRM in CLUPs is not an appendix—it is integrated into zoning and land allocation decisions.

questions.text: Which scenario best demonstrates the integration of climate resilience into disaster-responsive planning at the CLUP level?

options.text: A municipality creates a separate DRRM office that handles all disaster planning independent of the Planning Office, which may lead to coordination issues
A CLUP designates high-risk flood zones as no-build or restricted-use areas, restricts high-density development in earthquake-prone areas, and integrates evacuation corridors into the road network
A municipality invests heavily in post-disaster reconstruction funds without revising land use patterns, potentially leading to repeated damage
A CLUP is prepared, then DRRM is added as a separate supplementary document without modifying zoning, which may not fully integrate resilience

rationale.a: A separate office handles implementation but DRRM must be embedded in the CLUP itself for mainstreaming.
rationale.b: True disaster-responsive planning integrates hazard awareness INTO the zoning and land use framework itself: hazard-zone designations, use restrictions, infrastructure design. This is mainstreaming—making DRRM part of the planning fabric, not an add-on.
rationale.c: Post-disaster funding is reactive; resilience planning is preventive.
rationale.d: A supplementary document without zoning changes is not true mainstreaming; DRRM must reshape zoning decisions.
rationale.correct: True disaster-responsive planning integrates hazard awareness INTO the zoning and land use framework itself: hazard-zone designations, use restrictions, infrastructure design. This is mainstreaming—making DRRM part of the planning fabric, not an add-on.
rationale.takeaway: DRRM mainstreaming = DRRM integrated into zoning and land use restrictions, not handled separately.

questions.text: According to PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines), what is the easement requirement from the mean high tide line along seashores?

options.text: 3 meters for urban areas, 20 meters for agricultural areas, 40 meters for forest areas
20 meters for all coastal areas regardless of classification, ensuring uniformity in coastal management
40 meters for all coastal areas regardless of classification, to provide maximum protection against erosion
10 meters for all coastal areas, which is the minimum standard for environmental protection

rationale.a: PD 1067, Article 51 establishes an easement of public use along seashores with distances based on land classification: 3 meters in urban areas, 20 meters in agricultural areas, and 40 meters in forest areas.
rationale.b: 20 meters applies only to agricultural coastal areas, not uniformly to all coastal zones.
rationale.c: 40 meters applies only to forest areas, not uniformly to all coastal zones.
rationale.d: 10 meters is not a PD 1067 easement standard.
rationale.correct: PD 1067, Article 51 establishes an easement of public use along seashores with distances based on land classification: 3 meters in urban areas, 20 meters in agricultural areas, and 40 meters in forest areas. The same classification applies to rivers and streams based on width.
rationale.takeaway: PD 1067 easement distances vary by land classification: 3m (urban), 20m (agricultural), 40m (forest).

questions.code_citation: PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines, 1976), Article 51

questions.text: How does climate resilience planning address the World Bank estimate that disasters cost the Philippines approximately 1.9% of GDP annually?

options.text: By restricting development in high-hazard zones and investing in resilient infrastructure that reduces losses when disasters occur
By increasing disaster insurance costs to deter development in risky areas, thereby indirectly encouraging safer construction practices
By relocating all settlements away from hazard zones regardless of livelihood, which is considered impractical due to socio-economic impacts
By focusing only on post-disaster reconstruction, which is more cost-effective than prevention according to some outdated studies

rationale.a: Climate resilience planning reduces GDP loss by preventing development in high-risk zones and building resilience into approved development through design standards and setbacks. This front-loaded prevention is cost-effective compared to post-disaster recovery.
rationale.b: While insurance has a role, planning's primary tool is land use restriction and resilient design, not insurance pricing.
rationale.c: Planned development is possible outside hazard zones; absolute relocation is not the planning strategy.
rationale.d: Prevention through planning is far more cost-effective than repeated reconstruction cycles.
rationale.correct: Climate resilience planning reduces GDP loss by preventing development in high-risk zones and building resilience into approved development through design standards and setbacks. This front-loaded prevention is cost-effective compared to post-disaster recovery.
rationale.takeaway: The economic argument for climate resilience planning: prevention and resilient design cost less over time than managing repeated disaster impacts.

questions.code_citation: World Bank Philippines Disaster Risk Profile; Climate Resilience Planning

questions.text: A municipality with both active fault traces and coastal exposure is revising its CLUP. Which setback standards must be applied?

options.text: 5-meter fault setback OR 40-meter coastal setback, whichever is less restrictive, which may not ensure safety
Both 5-meter fault setback AND applicable PD 1067 easement (3/20/40m based on land classification) in their respective hazard zones
Only the 40-meter coastal setback, as it is more stringent, which may not address all hazards
Only the 5-meter fault setback, as geological hazards take priority over storm surge, which is not a comprehensive approach

rationale.a: Land use must satisfy ALL applicable hazard setback standards, not the least restrictive.
rationale.b: Different hazards have different setback standards. Both apply in their respective hazard zones: PHIVOLCS 5-meter fault setback, and PD 1067 easement distances (3m urban, 20m agricultural, 40m forest) along water bodies.
rationale.c: Both standards apply simultaneously in their respective zones; neither takes absolute priority.
rationale.d: Geological and meteorological hazards are equally significant in Philippine risk; both must be addressed.
rationale.correct: Different hazards have different setback standards. Both apply in their respective hazard zones: PHIVOLCS 5-meter fault setback, and PD 1067 easement distances (3m urban, 20m agricultural, 40m forest) along water bodies. A site may be subject to one or both restrictions depending on its location.
rationale.takeaway: Setback standards are cumulative by hazard type—a site must comply with every applicable standard for its location.

questions.text: A planner identifies that a proposed CLUP revision removes a 5-meter setback requirement from an active fault zone to permit affordable housing development. Under RA 10121, what is the correct response?

options.text: Approve the removal because housing need takes priority over hazard mitigation, especially in urban areas with high population density
Maintain the setback requirement; DRRM mainstreaming under RA 10121 makes hazard protection non-negotiable in planning decisions
Remove only the fault setback but maintain the coastal setback if applicable, ensuring compliance with local zoning ordinances
Refer the matter entirely to PHIVOLCS for final decision without planner involvement, as they have the expertise in seismic risk assessment

rationale.a: Housing need is important but cannot override life safety hazard protections. Alternative sites outside hazard zones must be sought.
rationale.b: RA 10121 mandates that DRRM be mainstreamed into CLUPs, making disaster risk reduction a non-negotiable planning obligation. Planners must balance development with resilience; setback requirements exist to protect life and property, not to arbitrarily restrict development.
rationale.c: If an area is subject to fault hazard, the setback applies regardless of other considerations.
rationale.d: While PHIVOLCS maps faults, planners have the responsibility to implement setback requirements in their CLUPs based on PHIVOLCS data.
rationale.correct: RA 10121 mandates that DRRM be mainstreamed into CLUPs, making disaster risk reduction a non-negotiable planning obligation. Planners must balance development with resilience; setback requirements exist to protect life and property, not to arbitrarily restrict development.
rationale.takeaway: DRRM mainstreaming under RA 10121 means that setbacks are binding planning constraints, not negotiable features.

questions.text: A coastal barangay proposes a new commercial fishing port facility 35 meters from mean high tide. The adjacent land is classified as agricultural. Based on PD 1067, is this compliant with easement requirements?

options.text: Yes, because the post-Yolanda framework allows commercial structures within 40 meters of the mean high tide line for livelihood purposes
No, because the 20-meter agricultural easement applies; the facility at 35 meters is outside the easement zone
Yes, because PD 1067 allows development within the easement for livelihood purposes such as commercial fishing port operations
No, because the post-Yolanda framework requires 40 meters for all coastal development regardless of land classification

rationale.a: The post-Yolanda framework does not establish a fixed 40-meter no-build zone; it recommends site-specific hazard assessment. PD 1067 provides the statutory easement.
rationale.b: PD 1067 establishes a 20-meter easement for agricultural coastal areas. The proposed facility at 35 meters is outside this 20-meter restriction and therefore compliant with PD 1067.
rationale.c: PD 1067 does not exempt livelihood structures from easement requirements; all structures within the easement zone are restricted.
rationale.d: The post-Yolanda framework does not establish a fixed 40-meter no-build zone; rather, it recommends hazard-based classification of areas. PD 1067 is the operative law.
rationale.correct: PD 1067 establishes a 20-meter easement for agricultural coastal areas. The proposed facility at 35 meters is outside this 20-meter restriction and therefore compliant with PD 1067. However, local zoning ordinances and site-specific hazard assessments (storm surge modeling) must also be considered.
rationale.takeaway: PD 1067 easement distances vary by land classification—20 meters for agricultural coastal areas. Site-specific hazard assessment is also required under DRRM mainstreaming.
